newsitem.title: USA: Fed meets amid expectations of steady U.S. rates.
newsitem.headline: Fed meets amid expectations of steady U.S. rates.

text.p: Federal Reserve policy-makers began a key meeting on the future of U.S. interest rates on Tuesday amid widespread expectations they would leave policy unchanged.

The U.S. economy is growing at a comfortable speed and there are few, if any, inflationary dangers in sight, giving the world's most powerful central bank little reason to change course, analysts said.

Evidence of a moderate U.S. housing market provided policy-makers with additional reasons to stand pat. The Commerce Department earlier Tuesday reported July housing starts were unchanged at an annualized 1.447 million-unit rate, slighty below market expectations.
The Fed's policy-maker Federal Open Market Committee began meeting at 9 a.m. (1300 GMT) The Fed's interest rate announcement was expected for 2:15 p.m. (1815 GMT).
Financial markets were firm ahead of the announcement.

At 10:30 a.m., the Dow Jones industrial average of Wall Street blue chip stock prices was up 13 points at 7,817, building on Monday's 108-point gain. The key 30-year Treasury bond was down 4/32, or $1.25 on a $1,000 bond, pushing its yield to 6.53 percent from Monday's close of 6.52 percent.

A group of 31 economists polled by Reuters earlier this week unanimously said they expected the Fed to keep the key federal funds rate -- what banks charge each other for overnight loans -- unchanged at 5.50 percent.

Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan last month said the central bank was scanning the economy closely and was ready to raise rates should any inflationary pressures emerge, but suggested it may be a while until that could happen.

The Fed has been particularly monitoring the tight labor market for signs of fresh wage pressures. Sweeping concessions won by the Teamsters union to settle a 15-day strike against United Parcel Service, the nation's largest package delivery company, are certain to be high on the Fed's agenda.
"As a psychological factor, it is certainly something that the Fed will be watching," said Alan Levenson, economist at Aubrey G. Lanston and Co. Inc.
Recent economic data strongly suggest growth is moderate and inflation is steady in the seventh year of U.S. economic expansion.
The Fed last changed interest rates March 25, when it raised the federal funds rate by 0.25 percentage point to pre-empt inflationary pressure.
It stood by at its last two rate meetings in May and July, convinced the U.S. economy would calm down by itself from its breakneck speed at the start of the year.

From a torrid 4.9 percent pace in the first quarter of the year, economic growth slowed to a more sustainable 2.2 percent in the April-July quarter as consumers reined in spending and inventories began to build up.

"Raising short-term rates at this time would be tantamount to putting on a raincoat and walking around with an oversized umbrella on a perfectly sunny day," said Anthony Chan, chief economist at Banc One Investment Advisors in Columbus, Ohio.
Economic growth is expected to pick up again in the third quarter, but analysts disagree on whether that would be sufficient to prompt the Fed to tighten credit again.
About two-thirds of the economists polled by Reuters projected the Fed would raise borrowing costs at least once before the end of the year.
Analysts said raising the cost of credit now would choke off the expansion prematurely and risk sending markets into a tailspin.
"I would be very surprised, even shocked, if the Fed did anything at this meeting," said Lyle Gramley, a former member of the central bank's Board of Governors.
